title: Can a Christian Lose Their Salvation?
excerpt: The New Testament promises that no one can snatch a believer from Christ's hand and warns believers not to fall away, often in the same chapter. The church has four ways of holding both, and one thing to say to the person who is afraid.
body:
A woman prayed to receive Christ at a summer camp when she was nine, and she has prayed the same prayer some two hundred times since, because she has never been sure the first one worked. A father sits in church beside the empty place where his son used to sit. The son was baptized at twelve, led the youth group's singing at sixteen, and at twenty-six says, without anger, that he doesn't believe any of it. A man who did something last year that he can't forgive himself for has been reading the sixth chapter of Hebrews at two in the morning.

All three are asking one question, and so is the skeptic who watches them. Christians say that salvation is a gift that cannot be earned. Many of them also say it cannot be lost. Yet they warn one another constantly about falling away, and their own Bible seems to warn them too. To the skeptic it looks like a promise with fine print. To the cynic it looks like something worse, a doctrine that lets a person pray once and then live as he pleases.

Something has to be said to the frightened reader before any of the argument. If you are lying awake afraid you have fallen away, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. The settled apostate does not agonize. If the fear has become too heavy to carry alone, tell a pastor or a friend you trust, and [Find Help](/help) lists places to turn. The last part of this essay is written for you, and you are free to go straight to it.

## The Promises

The promises are as strong as language can make them. "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me," Jesus says. "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand" (John 10:27–28). He goes on to say that the Father's hand is around his own, and that the Father "is greater than all" (John 10:29). Earlier in the same Gospel he states what he was sent to do: "this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day" (John 6:39).

Paul writes the same confidence into a chain with no broken link. "Those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified" (Romans 8:30). He ends the chapter by listing everything that might come between a believer and God, death and life, angels and rulers, the present and the future, and says that none of it "will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:39). To the church at Philippi he writes, "I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6).

Notice where each of these promises puts the weight. None of them says that the believer's grip is strong. They say that God's is.

## The Warnings

The warnings are as strong as the promises, and they stand in the same books.

The letter to the Hebrews was written to a congregation under pressure, some of whom were close to walking away from Christ. Its author tells them: "it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance" (Hebrews 6:4–6). Four chapters later he says it again. "If we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins" (Hebrews 10:26). He describes the person he has in mind as one who "has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified" (Hebrews 10:29).

The same Jesus who spoke of the sheep in John 10 speaks of the vine in John 15. "Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away," and "If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers" (John 15:2, 6). Peter writes of people who "have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ" and are "again entangled in them and overcome," and says "it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:20–21).

The New Testament does not keep these two kinds of text in separate rooms. Paul can put them in one sentence: "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you" (Philippians 2:12–13). He tells the Colossians that Christ will present them blameless "if indeed you continue in the faith" (Colossians 1:23). The short letter of Jude says "keep yourselves in the love of God" and, three verses later, gives glory "to him who is able to keep you from stumbling" (Jude 21, 24). And the author of Hebrews, straight after the most frightening paragraph in his letter, tells his readers, "in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things" (Hebrews 6:9), and ends the chapter with a hope that is "a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul" (Hebrews 6:19).

Any account of this question has to keep both sets of texts. The church's traditions differ on which set explains the other.

## How the Church Came to the Question

The church first met the question as a pastoral emergency. In the year 250 the emperor Decius required everyone in the empire to offer sacrifice, and thousands of Christians did. When the persecution ended they stood at the church door and asked to come back. A rigorist party said never. As this site's Study Bible notes, Tertullian had already used Hebrews 6 to argue that the church could not forgive grave sin after baptism. Cyprian, the bishop of Carthage, and the larger church said that the fallen could return through real repentance, tested over time. The first thing the church decided about falling away, then, was that a fall need not be final.

Augustine gave the question its lasting shape in the 420s. Against teachers who said that staying faithful is our own achievement, he argued that perseverance, like faith itself, is a gift of God. He also believed that some people are truly reborn and still do not receive that gift, and he did not claim to know why. If you grant that perseverance is God's gift, he told an opponent, "I think that equally with me you are ignorant why one man should receive this gift and another should not receive it." For Augustine, those whom God has chosen cannot be lost, and yet no one can read the list.

Every later position is an answer to that inheritance.

## Four Accounts, Each in Its Own Terms

The Catholic Church teaches that the grace given in baptism is real and can be lost by grave sin, and that it can be restored. The Council of Trent said in 1547 that the grace of justification is lost "not only by infidelity," but "by any other mortal sin whatever," and it gave a chapter to "the fallen, and their restoration" through the sacrament of penance. On perseverance it spoke with care: "let no one herein promise himself any thing as certain with an absolute certainty; though all ought to place and repose a most firm hope in God's help." A Catholic would say that this is what the warnings and the promises look like when both are kept. The Christian life is lived in firm hope and without presumption, and the door back stays open.

Lutherans agree that grace can be lost. Their first confession, presented at Augsburg in 1530, condemns those "who deny that those once justified can lose the Holy Ghost." But the Lutheran tradition puts the comfort in a different place. A troubled Christian is told to stop examining his own heart for evidence and to look at what God has said and done outside him: the promise of the gospel, his baptism, the bread and the cup. On this account you can fall by unbelief, and you are not kept by measuring your faith. You are kept by hearing the promise again.

The Reformed tradition holds that those whom God has truly made alive he keeps to the end. The Synod of Dort said in 1619 that believers, left to themselves, would certainly fall. That, it says, "is not only possible, but would undoubtedly happen." They stand "not in consequence of their own merits, or strength, but of God's free mercy." The Westminster Confession of 1646 states the conclusion: they "can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace." Those who leave for good, on this reading, show what John says of some who left his churches: "They went out from us, but they were not of us" (1 John 2:19). The Reformed read Hebrews 6 as describing people who shared every outward gift of the church's life and were never reborn. This teaching is often confused with the slogan "once saved, always saved," and it is a different thing. Its proper name is the perseverance of the saints, and it means that the saints persevere. The same confessions say that true believers can fall into grievous sin, and that assurance can be "shaken, diminished, and intermitted."

The Arminian and Wesleyan tradition holds that the warnings describe a real danger for real believers. The followers of Jacob Arminius left the question open in 1610 and later concluded that a true Christian can fall away. John Wesley preached of a man who "did receive the heavenly gift" and afterward "made shipwreck of the faith." In its own terms this is no doctrine of insecurity, and Wesley taught that a believer who continues in faith can have real assurance. God will keep anyone who remains in Christ, and no power outside the believer can take him away, which is what John 10 says. What God will not do is hold a person against his will, because the love he seeks is love freely given.

Other readings stand between these or beside them. Some Reformed scholars argue that the warnings are addressed to true believers and are the very means by which God keeps them, as a sign at a cliff's edge is one of the ways a father keeps his children from the cliff. Some evangelicals read the warnings as speaking of discipline or lost reward, and not of final loss. The site's notes on [Hebrews 6](/study/bible/hebrews/6) set these out more fully, and an earlier essay takes up the larger question of [election and free will](/writing/did-god-choose-me-or-did-i-choose-god) that lies under this one.

Each tradition fears something in the others. The Reformed fear a salvation that finally rests on the strength of the believer's own hold. The Wesleyan fears a teaching that turns the warnings into words no one needs to heed. The Catholic fears presumption. The Lutheran fears any answer that sends a sinner to look inside himself.

They agree on more than their arguments suggest. None of them teaches that God discards a believer for stumbling. None of them teaches that a prayer said once covers a life lived in settled contempt of Christ. All of them tell the person who is clinging to Christ that he is safe, and the person who has walked away to come back. They differ over how to describe the one who left. They give the same counsel to the one who is still here.

## What We Have Done

We have done damage on both sides of this, and often from the same pulpit.

We sold assurance cheaply. We counted raised hands and signed cards, told a child that a sentence prayed once had settled eternity, and then did not teach him to follow anyone. When he walked away at twenty we comforted ourselves with the card. That is the cynic's doctrine, and we are the ones who taught it. No confession of any church contains it.

And we terrified the tender. We preached the warnings to rooms full of the already anxious, asked them weekly whether they were sure, and watched the same people come forward again and again. We let Hebrews 6 be used on the grieving and the scrupulous, the people least like the ones it describes. We have also pronounced on other people's children, telling a mother what her son's unbelief proves about his baptism. Scripture gave us no such knowledge.

## If You Are the One Who Is Afraid

Hebrews 6 and 10 describe something specific. The person in view has trampled the Son of God underfoot and holds him up to contempt. That is a deliberate, settled renunciation of Christ. It is a different thing from doubt, from a season of coldness, from a sin you hate and keep committing. This site's note on the passage puts it this way. A person worried that they have committed such a sin shows, by that very concern, the tenderness toward God that the passage describes as absent.

Consider Peter. On the night of the arrest Jesus told him, "Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers" (Luke 22:31–32). Within hours Peter had denied three times, with an oath, that he knew him. Jesus had prayed for him before the failure, and had spoken of his return before he fell. On the beach after the resurrection he gave Peter his work back.

The Gospels are full of people whose faith was small and mixed. A father once said to Jesus, "I believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24), and Jesus healed his son. Matthew says of him, quoting Isaiah, "a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench" (Matthew 12:20). John tells anxious believers that "whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything" (1 John 3:20).

One more thing follows from what the traditions hold in common. Don't settle your anxiety by picking the doctrine that soothes it. Go back to the one who said he would not let go. Every one of these traditions would tell you the same.

And if you are the parent in the pew, none of these traditions claims to know the end of a life that is still being lived. The father in Jesus' story was still watching the road when his son was "a long way off" (Luke 15:20).

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess together that salvation is God's gift in Christ, received by faith and never earned, and that no one keeps himself by his own strength. They confess that God is faithful, that the warnings of Scripture are true and are meant to be heeded, and that a living faith follows Christ. Those belong to the faith itself.

Whether a person truly reborn can finally fall away is a question of the second order. Churches that recite the same creeds have answered it differently since the fifth century, and the [Honest Answer on this site](/answers/can-you-lose-your-salvation) says the same. This essay has set the answers side by side and does not choose among them.

Whether a particular person was ever a believer, or still is, or will be at the end, is not given to anyone to say.

The texts were never reconciled into a formula, and the people who trust Scripture most have noticed that it did not try. It tells those who are sure of themselves, "let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12). It tells those who have fallen that Christ prayed for Peter before Peter knew he needed it. Which of those two sentences a person needs to hear depends on where he is standing, and most of us have stood in both places. The question that began as "can I lose him" turns, when it is followed far enough, into a question about what kind of shepherd he is. The answer to that one was given on a cross, and it does not make the warnings less serious.

*"Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall."* (1 Corinthians 10:12)

*"All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out."* (John 6:37)
